capabilities.why: Student code is untrusted. A malicious submission can attempt to exfiltrate environment variables (LLM_API_KEY, CELESTO_API_KEY) via curl, wget, or a Python subprocess. By booting every grading sandbox with network_policy=off (internet completely disabled), we ensure that even if the safety hook missed a novel attack vector, no data can leave the microVM. This is the primary containment layer against prompt-injection exfiltration. Without it, a student who found our API key in the environment could drain our credits.

Safety hooks are Python callbacks that execute on the CONTROL PLANE before any command reaches the VM. Unlike a system-prompt instruction ('be careful'), a hook is compiled code that cannot be overridden by the model or a poisoned input. We block fork bombs, rm -rf /, dd disk writes, mkfs, and curl/wget commands carrying environment-variable references. Every command attempt — whether allowed or blocked — is written to logs/commands.jsonl with an ISO-8601 timestamp, sandbox name, decision, and execution_target=celesto_sandbox, giving a complete audit trail for post-incident forensics.

The grading pipeline checkpoints the sandbox state in step 6, immediately before executing untrusted student code in step 7. If step 7 fails — because the code crashes, hangs, is blocked by the safety hook, or triggers a ResourceExhausted error — we restore the pre-execution snapshot (rollback policy) rather than discarding all work and re-creating the VM from scratch. Rollback is faster than FreshStart (sub-second vs 30-60 s for a full VM rebuild) and safer than Resume (which would inherit the corrupted state). The snapshot is also the foundation for fork-and-explore parallelism in future work: clone the snapshot into N VMs, run N different grading strategies, keep the best score.
